description: The sentence "the cleanup in the `finally:` above still runs on that same thread, before the exception surfaces at the `await`" holds for an exception raised inside the threaded body but is false for the cancellation case the same paragraph describes. Because `asyncio.to_thread` cannot interrupt a running worker, a `CancelledError` surfaces at the `await` immediately while the thread's `finally` cleanup runs later. Capped behavior-inert by Phase 4.1.5 (first-conjunct held, limb-one held, limb-two held).

The inline comment repeats the same imprecision: "teardown runs on the thread that owns the connection, before any exception surfaces at the await". The thread-affinity half is correct; the "before any exception surfaces at the await" half is false under cancellation. The MySQL and Postgres runners carry no equivalent sentence. Capped behavior-inert by Phase 4.1.5.

The rewritten item attributes `loop.shutdown_default_executor()` to `uvicorn/_compat.py` while the issue's verified premise records that call in `uvicorn/server.py`. One agent could not check it (uvicorn is outside the workspace); prflow:comment-analyzer read the installed `uvicorn/_compat.py` 0.54.0 and reported the claim correct, so this stands only as an unresolved cross-check. Capped behavior-inert by Phase 4.1.5.

The added sentence asserts "so its health check keeps answering". `/healthz` is served only by the HTTP transport's path normalizer, while the preceding paragraph walks the reader through stdio mode, where no health endpoint exists. True for HTTP, vacuous for the adjacent stdio reader; the criterion asks only for the "does not stop the server from accepting other requests" part. Capped by Phase 4.1.5 at important (limb-two not held, docs/external is published), weighed at the lower of that and its original suggestion.

Every `False` return from the rollback logs one INFO line, but `BoundedConversationStore.truncate_messages` returns `False` for three distinct reasons. One of them, a user-id mismatch, means the conversation still exists and still holds the cancelled call's messages, a genuinely failed rollback that the sibling branch treats as ERROR-worthy. The log cannot distinguish the three. Unreachable today because the shipped resolver yields one user id.

`_ConversationQueueEntry` bundles a lock and a public mutable `users` counter but owns no behavior. Its refcount invariant is maintained by two module-level functions, hand-written arithmetic at two call sites, and a separate dict-registration site. `_release_queue_entry` tests `users <= 0`, folding a double release into the same branch as the correct zero case, so a future double-release would delete the entry silently. Behavior on the diff's paths is correct.

`truncate_messages` is declared only on `BoundedConversationStore`, not on the `ConversationStore` base class, so the production caller probes for it at run time and degrades to an ERROR log. Support for synchronous cancel rollback is therefore a runtime requirement rather than a typed one, and a type checker cannot warn an embedder that the framework default store loses the rollback.

`truncate_messages` deletes the tail of `conversation.messages` from outside the model, while `add_message` couples that list to `updated_at` by stamping both together. After a rollback `updated_at` still reflects the cancelled turn whose messages are gone, and that timestamp is the key `list_conversations` sorts on.

`_conversation_turn`'s yielded `str | None` carries two decisions at once (which id to roll back, and whether a lock was taken), and the caller keeps the baseline as two independently initialized locals with an empty string standing for "no baseline". An empty user id is a representable but illegal state kept from `truncate_messages` only by the `queued_id is not None` guard, where it would match no conversation and return `False` as a silently skipped rollback.

The comment above `_LIVENESS_TIMEOUT_SECONDS` and `_assert_loop_live_while`'s docstring both claim a pre-fix run fails by the `asyncio.wait_for` probe timing out, which cannot happen: `wait_for`'s timer runs on the same loop the blocking call would hold. On a pre-change tree the test instead fails on `assert not blocked.done()` after the fake driver's own thirty-second wait. The tests work; the stated reason is wrong and will mislead anyone tuning that timeout. Capped behavior-inert by Phase 4.1.5.

`test_profile_row_cap_reaches_offloaded_runner` pins the per-request profile row cap for `PostgresRunner` only. MySQL and SQLite gained the same `asyncio.to_thread` hop and each read `effective_row_cap` inside the thread, so switching either to `loop.run_in_executor` (the mistake all three in-code comments warn against) would silently fetch the base `max_rows` with no failing test. The liveness tests for those runners pass regardless of the cap.

The `stream_request` docstring still says it "Yields text chunks as they arrive", while the new implementation drains the whole stream on a worker thread and yields the collected text afterwards. The inline comment below it describes the new behavior correctly. Raised by the code-reviewer as a sub-threshold note. Capped behavior-inert by Phase 4.1.5.

_rollback_conversation guards the conversation store's missing truncate_messages method but not a call to it that raises. The lookup uses getattr(store, "truncate_messages", None) and logs at ERROR when absent, but the call at line 247 is unguarded. Its only caller is the except asyncio.CancelledError handler at lines 427 to 438, so an exception from that call would travel out of the handler and replace the cancellation the bare raise at line 438 propagates, with nothing recording that the rollback did not happen. The shipped BoundedConversationStore raises only ValueError for a negative length and the caller derives baseline_messages from len(...)-or-zero, so the shipped wiring cannot reach this path; an embedder supplying its own store could.

The two new helpers annotate the agent parameter as Any (_conversation_baseline at line 498, _rollback_conversation at line 516) although the value passed is always the Agent that get_agent returns in src/sqllens/tools/_agent.py line 44. The structural requirement this change introduces, a store with a synchronous truncate seam plus a user resolver, is expressed in no type: ConversationStore in src/sqllens/agent/core/storage/base.py declares only its five asynchronous methods, so a type checker cannot see the missing-method seam or a typo in an attribute name and the only signal is the run-time getattr probe. A narrow Protocol for the two attributes would make the dependency checkable.

The stream_request docstring still says the method "Yields text chunks as they arrive". After this change the whole stream is drained inside one asyncio.to_thread call and every chunk is yielded only after the stream has completed, which the inline comment four lines below describes correctly, so the docstring and the comment contradict each other.

The added sentence that the cleanup in the finally: block "still runs on that same thread, before the exception surfaces at the await" holds for an exception raised inside the threaded body but not for the cancellation case the surrounding paragraph is about. asyncio.to_thread cannot interrupt a running worker, so a CancelledError surfaces at the await immediately while the worker's teardown runs afterwards, which is what the bolded sentence just before it asserts. Also stored as checklist FAIL VC-17.

The inline comment repeats the same ordering claim, that "teardown runs on the thread that owns the connection, before any exception surfaces at the await". The thread-affinity half is correct; the ordering half is wrong under cancellation, where the await raises first and this finally block can run much later. The MySQL and Postgres runners carry no equivalent sentence.

The truncate_messages docstring lists three reasons for returning False and tells the reader this is "never an error". The user-mismatch case does not fit: the conversation still exists and still holds the cancelled call's messages, a failed rollback with the same consequence the sibling missing-method branch logs at ERROR. src/sqllens/tools/query_database.py lines 255 to 256 restate the claim and omit the same case, so the INFO log cannot be told apart from the harmless outcomes.

The sentence promises that "its health check keeps answering", but /healthz exists only in the HTTP transport's path normalizer, and the surrounding paragraph walks the reader through the stdio setup as well, the recommended Claude Desktop path two sentences earlier. The acceptance criterion asks only for the half saying a waiting question does not stop the server from accepting other requests; the unqualified health-check clause leads a stdio reader to expect an endpoint that is not there.
The added paragraph links to cleanup-error-handling.md twice in consecutive sentences. Both statements are true; the repeated link makes the paragraph read as though two different pages were meant.

_FakeStream.text_stream blocks on release.wait() inside the property getter, so the streaming liveness test pins that the event loop stays responsive while the stream object is obtained rather than while chunks are iterated. The real SDK blocks between chunks, inside the for loop. The test still fails against a tree without this change, so coverage of the first criterion holds; the fake is less faithful than the non-streaming and runner fakes, which block inside create and execute.

The new truncate_messages takes a raw user_id: str and compares conversation.user.id != user_id, while the sibling methods get_conversation, delete_conversation and list_conversations at lines 63 to 91 all take a User and unwrap the identity themselves. The one method that can delete data is the one whose caller is trusted to have already unwrapped it, so an unrelated string, including the empty string the caller initializes baseline_user_id to, is a well-typed argument that quietly matches no conversation and returns False, a skipped rollback. The length < 0 precondition is raised explicitly while this identity precondition is not.
